title: Optimize Console Walkthrough — Prefetch, Batching & KV Cache Strategy (Lakemount Systems)
summary: High-level Optimize console demo covering prefetch/prefix KV cache, batching tradeoffs, and a tailored cost model. Customer leaned toward Dedicated for PII workloads but wants cost SLOs and a pilot. Agreed next steps: share cost spreadsheet, run a 2-week sandbox with 10k sessions, schedule follow-up technical benchmark.
topics: Current infra and data residency needs
Traffic shape: short chats with long context lookups
Prefetch / prefix KV cache behavior and TTLs
Batching sizing and latency vs cost tradeoffs
Cost model walkthrough and sensitivity analysis
questions: How does Redwood Optimize estimate savings for mixed session lengths?
What are typical TTL values for prefix cache in similar customers?
Can we enforce SSO + audit logs in Private deployment?
How much tail-latency increases with batching at peak concurrency?
next_steps: Avery to send customized cost model sheet and sandbox invite by 2026-02-03
Ravi to provision a 2-week sandbox with 3 GPU nodes and sample trace ingest (Lakemount to provide traces) by 2026-02-10
Lakemount to share production traffic histogram and a redacted prompt sample by 2026-02-02

meeting_header:
Date: 2026-01-27
Time: 16:00 PST
Duration: 58 minutes
Location: Zoom
Recording: https://redwood.zoom.us/rec/share/abc123 (private)
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Redwood), Tom Gregor (Lakemount CTO), Maya Singh (Lakemount Head of ML), Evan Park (Lakemount Infra), Sophie Lane (Lakemount PM)
transcript:
[00:00] Avery: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I'm Avery from Redwood, AE on the account. We'll run a short Optimize console walkthrough focused on prefetch/prefix KV caching and batching recs, then look at a cost model.
[00:18] Tom: Thanks, Avery. We have about 45 minutes allocated, may be tight but good. Quick reminder, Lakemount is PII heavy so private deployment is on the table.
[00:28] Avery: Totally, we'll call out any Private/Dedicated constraints. Ravi, do you want to kick off with the console?
[00:33] Ravi: Yup, sure. I'll share my screen — give me one sec. (screen share noise) Okay, Optimize console in the left nav, the scenarios tab — we preloaded a sample trace you sent last week, labelled "lakemount-prod-sample".
[00:47] Maya: Quick note — that sample has a lot of short turn chats and a subset with long context lookups, so TTLs matter.
[00:55] Ravi: Right, so the first card is 'Prefix KV prefetch'. This is where we analyze candidate prefixes across sessions and suggest a TTL and prefetch probability to maximize hit-rate without over-fetch. The UI shows expected hit-rate vs request overhead.
[01:12] Sophie: How do you compute expected hit-rate? Is that simulation or a model?
[01:18] Ravi: Good question. It's a hybrid: we replay session traces through a prefix-selection heuristic, then estimate cache hit-rate given TTL/eviction policy and your concurrency shape. There is some sampling so numbers are approximate — usually within ±3–5%.
[01:33] Tom: That ±5% concerns me — at scale that could swing us a lot in the cost model. Can you show sensitivity?
[01:40] Ravi: Yup. Click 'Sensitivity'. (pause) We show a slider for TTL and one for batch size. The sheet updates nominal cost, latencies, and tokens saved. For your trace, prefetch TTL of 30s hits ~42% and 80s hits ~57%. The incremental network cost for prefetch is low because prefetch responses are mostly short embeddings or packed KV pages.
[02:05] Maya: Embeddings — are those stored in our KMS? How's encryption handled?
[02:11] Avery: On Private we integrate with your KMS/HSM and audit logs. For hosted or dedicated, we support envelope encryption and access controls. We'll share the security whitepaper after.
[02:22] Evan: If we do Private, does that change the prefetch behavior? Like prefetch hitting a customer-side cache vs Redwood remote?
[02:29] Ravi: Behavior is same logically; only the physical placement differs. On Private, prefetch reads/writes a local KV service you host, so network hop is internal and latency is lower — which actually improves the economics for shorter TTLs.
[02:45] Tom: So shorter TTLs become more attractive if Private. Good to know.
[02:50] Ravi: Exactly. Now batching: in the next panel we simulate batching across independent requests. We show per-token cost vs tail latency for different concurrency assumptions. For your traffic mix, a batch size bump from 1 to 4 reduces per-token infra cost by ~18% but increases p99 latency by ~30ms in our sim.
[03:11] Sophie: That 30ms p99 — is that measured or estimated?
[03:14] Ravi: Estimated using our runtime perf models and recent kernel benchmarks on the selected GPU type (A10s in this sim). For Dedicated/Private with A100s numbers will differ.
[03:23] Maya: We're sensitive to p99 — product SLAs expect less than 300ms end-to-end for most conversational flows.
[03:29] Avery: We can tune for latency-first rollouts: smaller batch max and tighter latency SLOs, or route latency-sensitive tenants to a low-batch pool and cost-sensitive to a high-batch pool. The console demo shows route policies.
[03:42] Tom: Route policies — can we split by user tier? We want enterprise customers on low-latency and freemium on cost-optimized.
[03:49] Ravi: Yep. Policy rules: token budget, model version, and tags you set. We'll add a sample policy for 'Enterprise' -> low batch cap, 'Freemium' -> 8 max batch.
[03:58] (short pause, typing)
[04:05] Maya: Back to prefetch — what's the typical TTL range you see for sessionized apps?
[04:10] Ravi: Usually 30–90s for conversational apps with some longer ones up to 5 min for ticketing/chatbot follow-ups. If your sessions re-attach after minutes, that's different and we recommend session-indexing not just prefix prefetch.
[04:22] Avery: Note: Our 'sessionization' feature groups redispatches into session windows. That helps reduce duplicate prefetches across reconnects.
[04:30] Tom: Could you demo the cost model for our production volume? We gave you a weekly token count and concurrency histogram in the sheet.
[04:36] Avery: Sure, open the Cost Studio tab — I uploaded a model that maps your histogram to infra and token costs and applies Redwood discounts. (switching) Here are three levers: batch size, prefetch TTL, and KV hit-rate. The right chart is an elasticity curve.
[04:52] Ravi: For Lakemount's baseline, estimate monthly infra cost $13.4k with no prefetch and batch size 2. With TTL 60s + batch size 4 and hit-rate 55% the model projects $9.8k — about 27% reduction.
[05:10] Evan: That's a big delta. How sensitive if hit-rate is off by 10%?
[05:14] Avery: If hit-rate is 45% instead of 55% cost cuts are ~18%, so it's still material. That's why we propose a short pilot to measure real-world hit-rate.
[05:26] Sophie: Pilot scope?
[05:27] Avery: A 2-week sandbox with sampled traffic, running the Optimize policies and instrumenting true hits, latencies, and edge cases. We'll produce a validated cost model after.
[05:37] Tom: Are there any limits on prefetch size? Could prefetch push a lot of token volume on spike?
[05:43] Ravi: We cap prefetch concurrency and set circuit breakers. Prefetch is async and we prioritize real user requests, so it won't starve live traffic. The console shows backpressure thresholds.
[05:52] Maya: Regarding storage, what's the eviction policy for KV? LRU? TTL-first?
[05:56] Ravi: By default TTL-first + size-based eviction. You can configure LRU if you prefer. We advise TTL-first for predictable cache staleness.
[06:06] Tom: Okay. Can we map out the success criteria for the pilot? I want clear go/no-go numbers.
[06:11] Avery: Suggested success criteria: >40% reduction in token-related infra spend or <10% p99 latency increase, 95% availability, and no security policy violations. We can adjust thresholds with you.
[06:23] Evan: Security policy violin.. I mean violations — what about audit logs and SSO? We need SAML SSO and an audit trail forwarded to our SIEM.
[06:31] Avery: Supported. We integrate with SAML/SSO, provisioning via SCIM, and audit logs can stream to your SIEM. We'll also provide SOC2/ISO docs.
[06:39] Tom: Good. Who owns configuration if we choose Private? We want admin-level RBAC split.
[06:45] Lena: On Private you manage the infra and we provide the control plane which can be colocated or remote depending on contract. RBAC is fine-grained — route-level, model-level, and token-level roles.
[06:56] Sophie: Back to console numbers — show me the 'what-if' where we prioritize latency and still try to get cost wins.
[07:01] Ravi: (clicks) Okay scenario 'latency-first'. We set batch cap 2, prefetch TTL 45s, and do route split: 30% traffic to low-latency pool. Result: cost savings drop to ~10% but p99 stays within 12ms of baseline.
[07:18] Tom: That seems reasonable. Is there a recommended rollout pattern? Canary? A/B?
[07:22] Avery: Canary with small percent and automatic rollback on latency regressions is common. The console supports canary weighting and automatic fallback to the previous model/pool if latency or error budget is exceeded.
[07:34] Maya: A few practicals: we have frequent zero-day model updates and occasionally change model sizes. How does Optimize adapt?
[07:41] Ravi: We track model signature changes and re-run the cost sim on new model profiles. If model size changes we update kernel selection and expected throughput; the console will flag increased token cost and give re-tuning suggestions.
[07:54] Evan: For the pilot, what GPUs do you emulate? We run on A100 in prod.
[07:59] Ravi: We can simulate A100 profiles — I used A10 earlier but pilot will run on configs you request. The sandbox can be provisioned with A100s to match your environment.
[08:09] Sophie: Any gotchas with batching + streaming responses? We stream partial tokens to clients and don't want large buffering delays.
[08:16] Ravi: Streaming and batching is supported. We use micro-batches for streaming joins so the first byte latency is still low. There's a tradeoff: smaller micro-batch gives faster first byte, larger batch better throughput. We show that tradeoff on the streaming tab.
[08:29] (someone coughs)
[08:32] Tom: Can we see a raw session replay that shows prefetch hits/misses?
[08:36] Ravi: Sure — open 'Session Explorer' -> pick a session. (pause) Here we show API call timeline, cache lookups, cache hits highlighted in green and misses in red, and per-call token counts. For this sample, about 52% hits for a specific agent.
[08:51] Maya: Some of our prompts contain user PII embedded; can prefix prefetch accidentally include PII in cache keys? That would be bad.
[08:58] Avery: We have scrubbers and token-masking rules; Optimize respects redaction patterns and supports custom regex filters so keys don't include PII. We'll include the redact rules doc.
[09:08] Evan: Nice. For the pilot, how invasive is instrumentation? We prefer a low-touch approach.
[09:13] Ravi: Minimal: you provide a trace sample (we can optionally stream live traces to the sandbox), and we add lightweight SDK hooks to annotate requests with session ids. No code changes to your model code required for read-only sims.
[09:26] Sophie: OK, talk money: is there a separate charge for Optimize or is it included?
[09:31] Avery: Optimize is part of the Console package for enterprise tiers; for sandbox/pilot it's included. Longer term it's a per-seat/platform add-on depending on retention and number of scenarios. We'll include pricing tiers in the follow-up email.
[09:44] Tom: Any competitor differentiation we can call out in the slide I show execs?
[09:48] Avery: Key points: runtime-optimized kernels + unified control plane across hosted/dedicated/private, cost-aware routing and built-in prefetch PKV analysis, and field-proven rollouts (canary + auto fallback).
[09:59] Maya: Are any of those features proprietary or do you rely on third-party tooling?
[10:03] Ravi: Our serving runtime and Optimize scoring are Redwood in-house; we integrate with standard infra pieces (KMS, Prometheus, SIEM) but core batch/caching heuristics are our IP.
[10:13] Tom: Good. Sophie — any product perspective questions?
[10:16] Sophie: One: how do you recommend we tune TTL given variable user behavior? Is dynamic TTL per-session possible?
[10:23] Ravi: Yes, adaptive TTL per-session based on session recency and user cohort is possible. The console has a 'dynamic TTL' toggle which uses a small ML heuristic — we can run it in shadow mode during your pilot.
[10:35] Maya: Shadow mode means no prefetch actual calls, just predictions?
[10:38] Ravi: Exactly — we log what we would have prefetched and measure predicted hit-rate vs actual. That reduces risk for the pilot.
[10:46] (short pause)
[10:50] Tom: Ok, let's talk timeline: if we get the sandbox by Feb 10 and run 2 weeks, can you promise a validated model by end of Feb?
[10:58] Avery: Yes, deliverable timeline looks like: 2/10 sandbox up, 2/10–2/24 run, 2/25 deliver validated cost model and recommendations.
[11:08] Evan: Who from your team will be our day-to-day contact during the pilot?
[11:12] Avery: Ravi will be the technical contact and Lena will own onboarding and analytics. I'll be overseeing the project as AE.
[11:19] Sophie: Any final blockers we should raise now?
[11:22] Maya: I'd like to confirm audit log format early so our security team can vet.
[11:26] Evan: And the SCIM/SSO mapping — mapping group attributes.
[11:30] Avery: We'll include the SIEM/audit log schema and SCIM mapping doc in the follow-up package.
[11:36] Tom: Sounds good. Let's wrap with meeting recap.
[11:39] Avery: Recap: we'll send cost model, spin up sandbox, Lakemount provides traces and sample sessions, security docs shared, follow-up benchmark week of 2/16.
[11:49] Sophie: Agree. Thanks everyone.
[11:51] Maya: Thanks — looking forward to the sandbox.
[11:53] Ravi: Thanks, bye.
[11:55] Tom: Bye.
